name: Linux Tracing Taxonomy
description: Mental model from Julia Evans (with Brendan Gregg's framing) for Linux's tracing landscape: split into three layers — data sources (kprobes / uprobes / tracepoints / USDT), collection mechanisms (ftrace / perf_events / eBPF), and user frontends (perf, bcc, bpftrace, ftrace shell wrappers, LTTng, SystemTap). Most confusion in Linux tracing comes from conflating these layers.

name: strace
description: Classic Linux user-space tool that traces syscalls made by a target process via the ptrace(2) interface. Very simple to use but has high overhead — every traced syscall causes two extra context switches. Per Julia Evans, often the favorite debugging tool despite the cost.

name: ltrace
description: Library-call tracer — traces calls into shared libraries (e.g., libc malloc, free, fopen) via ptrace. The library-level counterpart to strace's syscall view. Higher overhead than uprobes-based tools.

name: SystemTap
description: Pre-eBPF Linux tracing/scripting tool. Compiles a stap script into a kernel module loaded into the running kernel. Powerful and battle-tested but complex to set up; largely superseded by eBPF on modern kernels but still used on RHEL where stap has long-standing support.

name: LTTng
description: Linux Trace Toolkit Next Generation — high-performance kernel + user-space tracing system from Polytechnique Montréal. Optimized for low overhead and large trace volumes. Includes lttng-ust for user-space tracepoints. Used heavily in academic + telecom contexts; less common in general SRE work.

name: DTrace
description: Sun/Solaris dynamic tracing system from 2003 — the conceptual ancestor of eBPF-based tracing. Uses static probe points (USDT-equivalent) and a custom scripting language (D). Available on illumos, FreeBSD, macOS; Linux port exists but is largely superseded by bpftrace + eBPF.
